'''Paul Berg''' (June 30, 1926 – February 15, 2023) was an American [[biochemist]] and professor at [[Stanford University]].
He received the 1980 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] "for his fundamental studies of the biochemistry of [[nucleic acids]], with particular regard to recombinant-DNA".<ref name=Nobel> The other half went to [[Walter Gilbert]] and [[Frederick Sanger]] "for their contributions concerning the determination of base sequences in nucleic acids"{{cite web| title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1980| work=Nobel Foundation| url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1980/summary/}}</ref>

Berg received his undergraduate education at [[Pennsylvania State University|Penn State University]], where he majored in [[biochemistry]]. He received his PhD in biochemistry from [[Case Western Reserve University]] in 1952. Berg worked as a professor at [[Washington University School of Medicine]] and [[Stanford University School of Medicine]], in addition to serving as the director of the [[Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine]]. 

In addition to the Nobel Prize, Berg was presented with the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1983 and the National Library of Medicine Medal in 1986. Berg was a member of the Board of Sponsors for the ''[[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]]''.<ref name="OAC">{{cite web|url=http://www.oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/tf1x0n98jp/|title=Guide to the Paul Berg Papers|website=oac.cdlib.org|access-date=May 4, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171022163704/http://www.oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/tf1x0n98jp/|archive-date=October 22, 2017}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Berg was born in [[Brooklyn]], New York City. He was the son of a [[History of the Jews in Russia|Russian Jewish]] immigrant couple,<ref name=Moskal/> Sarah Brodsky, a homemaker, and Harry Berg, a clothing manufacturer.<ref name="stuffbio">{{cite web| url=http://science.howstuffworks.com/dictionary/famous-scientists/biologists/paul-berg-info.htm |title= HowStuffWorks 'Paul Berg' |website=Science.howstuffworks.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160520085045/http://science.howstuffworks.com/dictionary/famous-scientists/biologists/paul-berg-info.htm |archive-date=May 20, 2016 |date=October 21, 2008 |access-date=April 3, 2014}}</ref> Berg graduated from [[Abraham Lincoln High School (Brooklyn, New York)|Abraham Lincoln High School]] in 1943,<ref name="Hargittai">{{cite book | last=Hargittai | first=I. | title=The Road to Stockholm: Nobel Prizes, Science, and Scientists | publisher=Oxford University Press | year=2002 | isbn=978-0-19-850912-7 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SHhs74OSk34C&pg=PA121 | access-date=April 21, 2022 | page=121 |quote=Arthur Kornberg (M59), Jerome Karle (C85), and Paul Berg (C80) all went to the Abraham Lincoln High School in Brooklyn.}}</ref> received his Bachelor of Science degree in biochemistry from [[Penn State University]] in 1948 and PhD in biochemistry from [[Case Western Reserve University]] in 1952. He was a member of the [[list of Jewish fraternities and sororities|Jewish fraternity]], [[Beta Sigma Rho|ΒΣΡ]].<ref>{{citation |title=About – Beta Sigma Beta at Penn State |url=https://betasigmabeta.com/about/ |access-date=2023-02-24 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Research and career==

===Academic posts===
After completing his graduate studies, Berg spent two years (1952–1954) as a [[postdoctoral fellow]] with the [[American Cancer Society]], working at the Institute of Cytophysiology in [[Copenhagen]], Denmark, and the [[Washington University School of Medicine]], and spent additional time in 1954 as a scholar in cancer research with the department of microbiology at the Washington University School of Medicine.<ref name="nobelcv">{{cite web |date=February 7, 2005 |title=Curriculum Vitae - Paul Berg |url=http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1980/berg-cv.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050207085222/http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1980/berg-cv.html |archive-date=February 7, 2005 |access-date=April 21, 2022 |publisher=Nobel Foundation}}</ref> He worked with [[Arthur Kornberg]], while at Washington University.<ref name="stuffbio"/> Berg was also tenured as a research fellow at [[Clare Hall, Cambridge]].<ref name="ClareHall"/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Singer|first1=Maxine|last2=Berg|first2=Pam|title=Genes and genomes|date=1990|publisher=University Science Books|location=Mill Valley, Ca.|isbn=0935702172|page=xxviii|url=https://archive.org/details/genesgenomeschan00sing}}</ref>  He was a professor at [[Washington University School of Medicine]] from 1955 until 1959.  After 1959, Berg moved to [[Stanford University]], where he taught biochemistry from 1959 until 2000 and served as director of the [[Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine]] from 1985 until 2000.<ref name=nobelcv /> In 2000 he retired from his administrative and teaching posts, continuing to be active in research.<ref name=Carey>{{cite book|last1=Carey, Jr.|first1=Charles W.|title=American scientists|date=2006|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York, NY|isbn=978-0816054992|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=00r9waSNv1cC&pg=PA25}}</ref>

===Research interests===
Berg's postgraduate studies involved the use of radioisotope tracers to study [[intermediary metabolism]]. This resulted in the understanding of how foodstuffs are converted to cellular materials, through the use of isotopic carbons or heavy nitrogen atoms. Paul Berg's doctorate paper is now known as the conversion of [[formic acid]], [[formaldehyde]] and [[methanol]] to fully reduced states of methyl groups in [[methionine]]. He was also one of the first to demonstrate that folic acid and B<sub>12</sub> cofactors had roles in the processes mentioned.

Berg is arguably most famous for his pioneering work involving gene splicing of [[recombinant DNA]].<ref name="Berg">{{cite web|title=Paul Berg|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/paul-berg|website=Science History Institute|access-date=May 5, 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180221223915/https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/paul-berg|archive-date=February 21, 2018}}</ref> Berg was the first scientist to create a molecule containing DNA from two different species by inserting DNA from another species into a molecule.  This gene-splicing technique was a fundamental step in the development of modern [[genetic engineering]].  After developing the technique, Berg used it for his studies of viral chromosomes.<ref name=nobelspeech>{{cite web|title=Award Ceremony Speech|url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1980/presentation-speech.html|publisher=The Nobel Foundation|access-date=March 25, 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110123024859/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1980/presentation-speech.html|archive-date=January 23, 2011}}</ref>

Berg was a [[professor emeritus]] at Stanford.<ref name=nobelcv /> As of 2000, he stopped doing active research, to focus on other interests, including involvement in public policy for biomedical issues involving recombinant DNA and embryonic stem cells and publishing a book about geneticist [[George Beadle]].<ref name=bergpage>{{cite web|title=CAP – Paul Berg|url=http://med.stanford.edu/profiles/Paul_Berg/|publisher=[[Stanford University]]|access-date=March 25, 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110609192008/http://med.stanford.edu/profiles/Paul_Berg/|archive-date=June 9, 2011}}</ref>

Berg was a member of the Board of Sponsors of the ''[[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]]''.<ref name="OAC"/> He was also an organizer of the [[Asilomar conference on recombinant DNA]] in 1975.  The previous year, Berg and other scientists had called for a voluntary [[Moratorium (law)|moratorium]] on certain [[recombinant DNA]] research until they could evaluate the risks.  That influential conference did evaluate the potential hazards and set guidelines for [[biotechnology]] research.  It can be seen as an early application of the [[precautionary principle]].

===Awards and honors===
[[File:Queen Beatrix meets Nobel Laureates in 1983.jpg|thumb|center|upright=2.0|[[Queen Beatrix]] meets Nobel laureates in 1983, Mildred Levy and Paul Berg are second couple from the left]]

====Nobel Prize====
Berg was awarded one-half of the 1980 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]], with the other half being shared by [[Walter Gilbert]] and [[Frederick Sanger]].<ref name="nobelcv" /><ref name="Autobiography2006">{{cite web |date=March 4, 2006 |title=Autobiography - Paul Berg |url=http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1980/berg-autobio.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060304124119/http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1980/berg-autobio.html |archive-date=March 4, 2006 |access-date=April 21, 2022 |publisher=Nobel Foundation}}</ref><ref>[http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1980/berg-interview.ram Berg interview] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050418020608/http://nobelprize.org/chemistry/laureates/1980/berg-interview.ram|date=April 18, 2005}} from the Nobel Prize website</ref>   Berg was recognized for "his fundamental studies of the biochemistry of [[nucleic acids]], with particular regard to [[recombinant DNA]]", while Sanger and Gilbert were honored for "their contributions concerning the determination of base sequences in nucleic acids."<ref name=1980nobel>{{cite web|title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1980|url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1980/|publisher=The Nobel Foundation|access-date=March 25, 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110305190238/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1980/|archive-date=March 5, 2011}}</ref>

====Other awards and honors====
He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and a member of the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1966.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter B|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=June 16, 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725002054/http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|archive-date=July 25, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul Berg |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/paul-berg-m4xsnj/ |access-date=May 31, 2022 |website=nasonline.org}}</ref> In 1983, [[Ronald Reagan]] presented Berg with the [[National Medal of Science]]. That same year, he was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Paul+Berg&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=May 31, 2022 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> In 1989, he received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> He was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1992|Foreign Member of the Royal Society (ForMemRS) in 1992]].<ref name=formemrs>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151112183951/https://royalsociety.org/people/paul-berg-11071/|archive-date=November 12, 2015|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/paul-berg-11071/|title=Professor Paul Berg ForMemRS|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London}}</ref> In 2005 he was awarded the [[Biotechnology Heritage Award]] by the [[Biotechnology Industry Organization]] (BIO) and the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]].<ref name=CHF>{{cite web|title=Biotechnology Heritage ==Death==
Berg died on February 15, 2023, at the age of 96.<ref name=Moskal>{{cite web|url=https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2023/02/nobel-paul-berg-obit.html|title=Nobel Prize winner and recombinant DNA pioneer Paul Berg dies|work=[[Stanford University School of Medicine]]|first=Emily|last=Moskal|date=February 21, 2023|access-date=February 18, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Paul Berg, pioneer in gene splicing who led way for biotech, dies at 96|language=en-US|newspaper=The Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2023/02/18/paul-berg-dna-nobel-dies/|access-date=February 20, 2023|issn=0190-8286}}</ref>
